Neonates of the Chinese skate are born with a disc width of approximately 10 centimeters [Lb = approximately 10 centimeters], a size that reflects the considerable yolk reserves allocated during oviducal gestation and that is typical for Dipturus species, conferring an immediate survival advantage over the smaller offspring of many other rajids. Upon emergence, these pups begin an independent existence, immediately commencing exogenous feeding on small benthic invertebrates within the shallow nursery grounds typical of the species. Growth during the first year is relatively rapid, although the ultimate total length attained by adults in the population reaches 83.1 centimeters [Li = 83.1 centimeters], a figure that represents the maximum recorded total length for this species in wild-caught specimens. Males, however, exhibit a somewhat smaller maximum size, with the ultimate total length for males capped at 76.8 centimeters [Li = 76.8 centimeters], a dimorphism that is common among many skates of the genus Dipturus. This ultimate size is not usually reached until well after the onset of reproductive maturity, as somatic growth continues slowly but steadily throughout much of the animal's life, albeit at a decelerating rate. Field surveys along the continental shelf of the East China Sea have consistently documented these maximum lengths from trawl-caught individuals, providing a robust empirical foundation for the growth parameters used in life-history models for this commercially important batoid.

Sexual maturation in female Chinese skates occurs when they reach a total length at puberty of 55.3 centimeters [Lp = 55.3 centimeters], a size that corresponds to an estimated age of approximately 9.4 years based on vertebral banding patterns. Males, in contrast, undergo sexual maturation at a smaller body size, with the total length at puberty for males recorded at 49.4 centimeters [Lp = 49.4 centimeters]. This divergence in length at maturity between the sexes is thought to reflect the different energetic demands placed on females, which must accommodate the development of large, yolk-laden eggs within their body cavity prior to copulation and subsequent egg-laying. Histological examination of gonadal tissue confirms that these lengths correspond definitively to the initiation of spermatogenesis in males and the onset of ovarian follicular development in females, marking the transition from the juvenile stage to the reproductively active adult phase of the life cycle. Such size-based thresholds are critical for fisheries management, as they help define the minimum legal catch size necessary to protect the breeding stock.

Under standard laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the age at birth for captive-born pups has been determined to be approximately 244 days [ab = approximately 244 days], a period that encompasses the entire duration of internal embryonic development following clasper-mediated fertilisation. This relatively protracted gestation period is consistent with the production of large, well-yolked eggs that give rise to fully formed, free-swimming neonates at parturition. The same thermal regime also governs the estimated maximum reproductive rate, which can be expressed as approximately 40 egg capsules per year [Ri = approximately 40 egg capsules per year], with each capsule containing a single pup [N_R_i = each capsule containing a single pup]. This maximum reproductive rate is achieved only at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], and field observations suggest that females in the wild may approach this rate only during the warmest months when prey resources are most abundant and metabolic conditions are favourable. Data from captive breeding colonies indicate that females achieving this maximum rate can deposit one egg capsule containing a single pup approximately every nine days during the peak of the reproductive season.

Longevity data for the Chinese skate, derived from both captive records and mark-recapture studies in the wild, indicate that maximum lifespan in the species reaches approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years], with the oldest documented individual recorded at this age before succumbing to nat at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]ural mortality. This lifespan, observed under the same thermal conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] that prevail in much of the species' temperate range, suggests a life-history strategy characterized by relatively slow growth, delayed maturation, and extended reproductive output across multiple years. The species thus conforms to the classic K-selected profile typical of many large-bodied elasmobranchs, where high juvenile survival and low natural mortality in adulthood offset the relatively modest fecundity. Comparative data from other members of the Rajidae family show that such lifespans are typical for skates of comparable body size, although some deeper-water congeners may live considerably longer. The combination of a late age at maturity and a moderate lifespan makes the Chinese skate particularly vulnerable to overexploitation.

The combination of late maturation at approximately 55.3 centimeters total length and a moderate lifespan of around 13 years directly influences the species' vulnerability to fishing pressure, as individuals must survive for nearly a decade before contributing to the next generation. Under optimal thermal conditions of 15 °C, a female achieving the maximum annual output of approximately 40 egg capsules per year [Ri = approximately 40 egg capsules per year] would deposit roughly 520 capsules over her reproductive lifespan, each yielding a single pup [N_R_i = each yielding a single pup] with an initial disc width of approximately 10 centimeters [Lb = approximately 10 centimeters] at birth. This lifetime fecundity, while modest in absolute terms compared to many teleost fishes, is typical for a late-maturing, relatively long-lived batoid and underscores the importance of protecting mature females to ensure population persistence. As a result, effective fisheries management for Dipturus chinensis must account for the slow life-history pace dictated by these key demographic parameters.
